title: Emrys and the Songbook
premise: Emrys Vasquez, a former prodigy cellist whose hands froze mid-concert a decade ago, agrees to a fake date with ferry mechanic Wren Calloway to survive a family reunion on a remote island where his estranged mother is selling the family inn. What begins as a performance becomes real, but Wren is hiding that she was the girl in the audience the night Emrys's career collapsed—and that she wrote the anonymous letter that ended his engagement. When a storm strands them past the last ferry, Emrys must finally say the apology he has rehearsed for ten years, choosing truth and Wren over the safe silence he has survived in ever since.
about_author: Gideon Nystrom is the pen name of a former orchestra librarian who spent fifteen years touring with chamber ensembles before turning to fiction. They write love stories set in the liminal spaces between performances, ferries, and the people we almost told the truth to.

chapters.title: The Broken Bow
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Ten years after his hands froze mid-concert, Emrys teaches cello to children who don't know his name and refuses every invitation home. When his sister texts that their mother is selling the inn, the emotional beat is dread: the past is calling collect.

chapters.title: A Plus-One for Hire
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Desperate for a shield at the reunion, Emrys meets Wren Calloway, a ferry mechanic who fixes his car and offers, half-joking, to pose as his boyfriend for gas money and a free weekend. The beat is wary hope disguised as a transaction.

chapters.title: Contract Terms
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren negotiates the fake-dating terms with brisk humor, but her internal monologue reveals she recognizes Emrys's name instantly—and says nothing. The beat is a secret planted: Wren was there the night everything broke.

chapters.title: Crossing to Merrow Island
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The ferry ride to the island is charged with rehearsal of their cover story, hands almost touching on the rail. Emrys narrates his family's landmines; Wren memorizes them. The beat is intimacy growing under the cover of performance.

chapters.title: The Inn at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Arrival at the crumbling inn; his mother greets Wren with startling warmth and Emrys with careful distance. His sister suspects the relationship instantly. The beat is the ache of being a stranger in your own childhood home.

chapters.title: Rules of Engagement
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. First shared bedroom, first coordinated lies at dinner. Wren plays the role flawlessly but keeps cataloguing real details about Emrys—the way he taps rhythms when anxious. The beat is the fake beginning to feel dangerously easy.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. At the reunion dinner, under pressure from a probing aunt, Emrys kisses Wren to sell the story—and forgets, for three full seconds, that it's fake. The beat is the blurb's hinge: too real by dessert.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brought In
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Morning beach walk; Wren nearly confesses she knows about the concert but deflects with a story about her own family she lost. Emrys offers her the found family she never had. The beat is mutual longing with a crack of guilt.

chapters.title: The Songbook in the Attic
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Packing the inn, Emrys finds his childhood songbook—full of compositions he never played for anyone, including a piece titled for a girl he never met. Wren reads a page over his shoulder and goes pale. The beat is the past surfacing.

chapters.title: The Anonymous Letter
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Flashback chapter: the night of the catastrophic concert, the frozen hands, and the letter Wren wrote to Emrys's then-fiancé that ended the engagement. Wren has carried it for a decade. The beat is the secret's full weight revealed to the reader.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The sister confronts Emrys: she found Wren's name in old concert programs—front row, the night he broke. Emrys dismisses it as coincidence, but doubt takes root. Meanwhile, the forecast turns. The beat is rising tension on two fronts.

chapters.title: Repair Work
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren repairs the inn's ancient generator with Emrys's help; working side by side, they trade real confessions about failure and fear—everything except the one truth. The beat is closeness deepening precisely because of what's unsaid.

chapters.title: The Ferry Stops Running
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The last ferry of the season departs without them; the storm strands everyone. Emrys's mother, packing up the inn, asks him to play something one last time in the empty dining room. He almost does. The beat is the door to the past closing literally.

chapters.title: Candlelight and Confessions
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Power out, the family gathers by candlelight. Emrys's mother tells the story of the concert from her side—she was there, and she never blamed him. Wren, hearing it, realizes her letter may have cost him more than a career. The beat is guilt cresting.

chapters.title: The Sister's Evidence
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. His sister shows Emrys the old playbill: Wren's name, front row. Then a second document—a copy of the anonymous letter, kept by the ex-fiancé, that the sister tracked down. The handwriting is Wren's. The beat is betrayal detonating.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys confronts Wren in the storm-lashed boathouse. She admits everything: she was there, she wrote the letter, she took this job to finally face him. He walks into the rain. The beat is the climax's first strike—love and truth at war.

chapters.title: Why She Wrote It
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Alone, Wren unpacks the full truth: the fiancé was cheating, the letter was meant to save Emrys, and the timing was catastrophic accident, not malice. She decides to leave on the morning supply boat rather than hurt him again. The beat is sacrifice shaped like retreat.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Emrys finds the songbook open to the piece he never played and finally understands what his silence cost everyone, including Wren. He rehearses the sentence he has practiced for a decade—I'm sorry, and I forgive you—and runs for the dock. The beat is the choice.

chapters.title: Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the dock in the storm's aftermath, the supply boat idling, Wren hears a cello—the songbook piece, played imperfectly and alive. Emrys says the sentence. She steps off the boat. The beat is the climax resolved in truth, not performance.

chapters.title: What Survives the Storm
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. The family helps salvage the inn's salvageables; mother and son finally speak plainly about the decade of distance. The sister apologizes for detonating the letter, and Wren is folded into the family without ceremony. The beat is found family made real.

chapters.title: First Chair
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Spring: Emrys accepts a teaching residency and performs again—small hall, no stakes, hands steady. Wren sits front row, this time with his knowledge and welcome. The beat is the price of survival finally paid and refunded in love.

chapters.title: The Song He Kept
chapters.summary: Emrys's POV. Epilogue at the reopened inn. Emrys plays the songbook piece for a room of family and islanders, dedicating it to the girl in the front row who waited a decade for the truth. The beat is quiet, earned joy: love in the present tense at last.
